answer: The terms put everything that isn't MySQL, Postgres or Oracle under one blanket (like sorting people into 'technical' and 'non-technical', unfair to the second group), hiding real differences; you should name the specific type. 'NoSQL databases scale' is wrong as a blanket statement: you can build a non-relational database that doesn't scale at all, and the ones that do scale, scale for a very specific workload (Cassandra, MongoDB, DynamoDB each for a specific workload). Most were built to solve very specific problems.
evidence: Ch1 §1.1: 'There shouldn't really be a term like non-relational or NoSQL at all. It puts everything that isn't MySQL, Postgres or Oracle under one blanket...' 'As a blanket statement it is wrong. You can build a non-relational database that doesn't scale at all ... Cassandra scales, but for a very specific workload.'

answer: As a very broad separation that is not always true, they give up consistency (strong/CAP consistency) to get scalability and availability: with multiple nodes they scale horizontally and stay highly available.
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'non-relational databases typically give up consistency to give you scalability.' Board: 'In most cases, NoSQL databases provide scalability and availability by compromising consistency.'

answer: ACID consistency: the data stays correct, the database moves from one correct state to another. CAP consistency: visibility, once you write data it is available to query right away (strong consistency; precisely linearizability). NoSQL databases give up the CAP one (strong consistency).
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'consistency in the CAP theorem is different from consistency in ACID ... Consistency in ACID is about the data being correct ... Consistency in the CAP theorem is about visibility ... That is strong consistency, and it is the consistency non-relational databases give up.'

answer: Relational databases wanted all the data in one place, in one database instance; if that instance goes down the whole system is down, so it isn't highly available (in practice standby replicas can take over). Non-relational databases spread data horizontally, so if one node fails others still serve and there is almost never complete downtime. The price is strong consistency: most become eventually consistent (a write shows up everywhere but not at once), with exceptions since nothing is standardised, e.g. DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads by default, ConsistentRead=true for strongly consistent at twice the read cost).
evidence: Ch1 §1.2: 'Relational databases wanted all the data in one place, in one database instance. If that instance goes down, the system is down ... They become eventually consistent ... Most non-relational databases are eventually consistent, but you will always find exceptions ... DynamoDB is a good example of an exception.'

answer: The boxed statement: 'NoSQL DBs scale does not mean SQL does not → anything that shards, scales.' It is a big misconception that relational databases don't scale. Backed by Lecture 03's key-value store on MySQL, sharded by key range: keys A–M on one database, N–Z on another, which gave an almost highly available, horizontally scalable system at the cost of (cross-shard) consistency. (Also in ch5 the board, in pink, said these scaling properties can also be achieved on SQL databases, so saying SQL does not scale is not entirely correct.)
evidence: Ch1 §1.3: 'The class board boxed it: NoSQL DBs scale does not mean SQL does not → anything that shards, scales.' 'In Lecture 03 (§5.3, range shards) the key-value store on MySQL was split across databases: one held the keys from A to M, the other the keys from N to Z.' Ch5 §5.1: 'in pink: We can also achieve [these] on SQL databases. So, saying SQL does not scale is not entirely correct.'

answer: Properties given on the page: closest to relational; mostly JSON-based (no hard rule); support complex queries (aggregations in MongoDB, faceted queries in Elasticsearch) / querying on attributes of a document; partial updates. answer: They typically adopt a document database, because it gives almost the features the relational database gave (close to relational, though not as powerful). You almost never see a team jump straight to a key-value store, which is far more restrictive (only key-wise access, no peeking into the value).
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'when a team moves a generic relational schema off SQL, it typically adopts a document database, because that gives it almost the features the relational database gave. You will almost never see a team jump straight to a key-value store.'

answer: Partial update: update just one attribute of a document in place (e.g. $set settings.tz = 'IST'), nothing else touched. In a key-value store the value is an opaque blob, so you read the whole value, update it yourself and write the whole value back; no partial update (exception: Redis hashes with HSET).
evidence: Ch2 §2.1: 'you can make partial updates: in this document, update just this one attribute.' §2.3: 'The value is a blob. If you want to update it, you read it, update it and write it back. No partial update is possible ... Redis hashes let HSET set individual fields'.

answer: DynamoDB is a key-value store, not a document database, yet it still lets you query within the document (it supports both key-value and document models). Builders keep entering each other's space. Instead, focus on the access pattern and the features you need (complex queries, partial updates) and which database gives them.
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'DynamoDB is a key-value store, not a document database, yet it still lets you query within the document ... So understand the access pattern and the features ... What you need to know as an engineer is which features you want from a database and which database gives you them.'

answer: MongoDB: it started out saying 'we are BASE, not ACID'; now it is ACID compliant (maybe not as optimally as the SQL world, but compliant).
evidence: Ch2 §2.2: 'MongoDB is the example. It started out saying we are BASE, not ACID. Now MongoDB is ACID compliant, maybe not as optimally as the SQL world, but compliant.'

answer: Only key-wise operations: get a key, put a key, delete a key, insert a key, insert a value into the set at a key (GET, PUT, DEL, SET, SADD); never peek into the value. Examples: Redis, DynamoDB and Aerospike.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'Examples are Redis, DynamoDB and Aerospike ... Every operation you make, reads, writes, deletes, all of them, is key-wise: get a key, put a key, delete a key, insert a key, insert a value into the set at a key.'

answer: Every key-value operation names one key, so it lands on one shard and never needs a cross-shard query; it can be partitioned into thousands of partitions without hiccups. Richer query models (range operations, IN operator, complex queries) can touch many shards and must wait for all of them, a very expensive cross-shard query; the more complex the queries, the less you can distribute the data.
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'Because everything is key-wise, you can shard the database very easily: you never have to make a cross-shard query ... Cross-shard queries come from range operations and the IN operator ... The more complex the queries, the less you can distribute the data.'

answer: By limiting access (key-wise only), you get massive parallelism / partitioning and best performance (and availability); you pay with restricted access, losing the power of complex queries. Every single thing is a trade-off. (The page doesn't show the board's exact two bullets.)
evidence: Ch2 §2.3: 'A key-value store is the other extreme: by limiting access, you get massive parallelism ... You get the best performance, and you pay for it with restricted access.' Table: 'What you give up: The power of complex queries; you gain parallelism and availability'.

answer: Row store: each row's five values (R1, R2, R3) are stored next to each other as one long strip, row after row. Column store: values of each column are stored together in blocks c1 symbol to c5 timestamp, so each row (R1, R2, R3) is one cell in every column block, crossing every block.
evidence: Ch3 Fig 3·a: 'In a row store, the five values of each row, R1, R2 and R3, are stored next to each other as one long strip. In a column store, the values of each column are stored together, c1 symbol through c5 timestamp, so row 1 is one cell in every column block.'

answer: A very crude, very naive picture: one separate file per column; line n of each file holds that column's value for row n (e.g. three rows give a three-line file for column 1, then a file for column 2, and so on).
evidence: Ch3 §3.1: 'A very crude, very naive way to picture it ... one separate file per column. Line 1 of each file holds that column's value for row 1, line 2 holds row 2'.

answer: In a row store the row is the unit on disk: each row's columns are stored together, so the engine reads the whole row and then picks out the needed columns; it can't jump to the next row's price without passing over the rest of the row to know where it ends. For a 100-column table it 'will go row by row reading all columns & discarding 98 of them', wasting disk IO.
evidence: Ch3 §3.2: 'You didn't project them in the SELECT, but the engine still has to skim through them to get to the next row. The board put the 100-column version bluntly: a row database will go row by row reading all columns & discarding 98 of them ... Because the row is the unit on disk.'

evidence: Ch3 §3.2: 'On a column store the same query reads exactly two files, price and timestamp. It does no disk IO at all for symbol, name and exchange.'

answer: Both are fine. Many expose edge servers directly (in the class's view no harm; big companies publicly expose edge IPs), or you put them behind a load balancer. Trade-off: a public edge server can be attacked (must be hardened, no secrets on it), while a load balancer adds one more hop, about 3–5 ms per relay hop by the instructor's estimate ('about five milliseconds'), and WebSocket connections behind it are always sticky (one connection client to LB, one LB to server). For ultra-low-latency real time such as streaming a live class, expose the IPs directly; if the extra latency is acceptable, use the LB. Behind an LB the edge server can be private and call internal APIs (e.g. membership checks). Page note: Slack itself fronts its WebSocket servers with Envoy proxies.
evidence: Ch9 §9.4: 'A lot of people expose edge servers over the internet ... you can also put them behind a load balancer ... every relay hop adds about three to five milliseconds ... If that latency is acceptable, use the load balancer; if not, keep it public. Both are fine.'

answer: Harden it and put it through a very high security review: change the route tables, hide all ports, prevent SSH, block a lot of things on the machine. Never put credentials on it: zero credentials, it never talks to the database directly and doesn't know what it is; it holds only a Kafka connection string (page note: make it least-privilege, e.g. write-only to one topic, and have consumers validate). A simple rate limiter against DDoS (page note: infrastructure-layer floods need upstream network capacity).
evidence: Ch9 §9.4: 'it is hardened and goes through a very high security review: you change the route tables, hide all the ports, prevent SSH ... whenever a server is exposed on the internet, you don't put any credentials on it.'

answer: All you lose is the Kafka connection string, and Kafka is internal to the infrastructure, so no one outside can talk to it; with nothing critical on the server, the worst an attacker can do is a DDoS (they only get a machine that tells them edge server IPs), which a simple rate limiter can prevent. Page caveats: a Kafka credential is still a secret (an attacker could inject messages consumers trust and persist), so give the edge a least-privilege, write-only credential and validate in consumers; a rate limiter handles only some floods, SYN floods and UDP reflection need upstream network capacity.
evidence: Ch9 §9.4: 'If the server is compromised, all you lose is that string, and the Kafka is internal to the infrastructure ... the worst an attacker can do is a DDoS ... a simple rate limiter can prevent a DDoS.' Plus the two 'More precisely' notes.

answer: From the user, who takes the action: you always join a channel while online, so the client sends an event to its own edge server ('now I'm subscribed to this channel'); it doesn't go to every server, each edge server handles its own users' events. evidence: Ch8 §8.5 'How servers learn about channel changes': 'From the user, who is the one taking the action ... Creating a channel shows the whole loop ...'

answer: Instead of relying on the client, the edge server itself calls the backend API periodically and pulls which of its connected users are in which channels. evidence: Ch9 §9.4: 'Another is for the edge server itself to call the backend API periodically and pull which of its connected users are in which channels. That can't be done from a publicly exposed server; it can if the server is private.'

answer: Redis isn't required: the requirement is a real-time Pub/Sub (send messages in real time to everyone subscribed); any provider, database, tool or framework offering it, or one you build, would do. evidence: Ch8 §8.4 'Why Redis?': 'The requirement is real-time Pub/Sub, not Redis ... The instructor picked Redis because he has used Redis to build this exact same system'.

answer: No expiration, because there is no persistence: nobody stores the message anywhere; it is received and sent on to everyone subscribed.
evidence: Ch8 §8.4: 'There is no expiration, because there is no persistence: no one stores the message anywhere.'

answer: Don't trust the client's claims when membership is critical (private channels): a malicious user could claim membership and receive messages. Make the edge server private behind a load balancer and have it check membership with a backend API (or the database) before serving private channels. Relying on the client is fine while membership isn't sensitive. (The instructor called it a man-in-the-middle attack and designed it so on purpose; the page notes it is really broken access control: deny by default, check membership server-side.)
evidence: Ch9 §9.4 'Trusting the client's membership': 'if membership is critical, as with private channels, don't trust the client. Rely on a backend API call for membership: make the edge server private, put it behind a load balancer'.

answer: Calling such a service for every message to find where it goes is far too expensive, and then it is not real time any more. Even if it cached user data it's still a network call every time. It's overkill: keep it simple and store the routing information on the edge server itself.
evidence: Ch8 §8.6 'A tempting idea: a routing service': 'Making a call to that service every time ... is far too expensive, and then it is not real time any more ... store this routing information on the edge server itself.'

answer: Persistence is guaranteed (messages once sent will always be persisted); the real-time notification to other users is not: Redis Pub/Sub keeps nothing, so a message may be lost while Redis passes it to an edge server, and the user sees it when they refresh (or via the correction job). For an enterprise app, guaranteed persistence is what matters more.
evidence: Ch9 §9.3: 'So in this system the message is guaranteed to be persisted, but the notification to the other users isn't? Correct.'

answer: Not one Redis instance but a cluster of Redis (sharded, with intelligent balancing); and the Balancer keeps each organisation's users on the same edge server so most of that traffic never reaches Redis.

answer: They are not the same, and the difference isn't simply 'Kafka is asynchronous'. Kafka is pull-based (consumers pull) and keeps historical messages (for a retention window); Redis Pub/Sub pushes to everyone connected and has zero persistence (an offline subscriber misses it, at-most-once). Neither is superior: for real time Redis is superior, for persistence Kafka is; it is very contextual.
evidence: Ch8 §8.4 'Redis Pub/Sub vs Kafka': 'Kafka is pull-based ... Redis Pub/Sub pushes ... Nothing is superior and nothing is inferior. For real time, Redis is superior; for persistence, Kafka is.'

answer: No. The message goes out to users as a real-time notification immediately; only the storage is delayed ('Not delivered, stored'). The real cost: until persisted, the source of truth doesn't have it, so a user who refreshes won't see a message they already saw in real time.

Depending on the guarantees, you alter the approach.

answer: A user can just change their clock, e.g. to 1 January 1970; whatever time is on the database is the source of truth. Nor do you need client precision: messages from one client are never sent at exactly the same time, and latency-induced reordering is fine.
evidence: Ch10 §10.2: 'a user can just change their clock, to 1 January 1970 if they like ... Nor do you need the client's precision.'

answer: CRDTs to merge/resolve conflicts plus vector clocks on the client side, each client's vector clock persisted in the DB. Not worth it: maintaining vector clocks and doing merges on read slows the entire system, no one does it, and you don't re-architect for one edge case; a globally consistent vector clock per client is a massive problem; and vector clocks give only a partial causal order (concurrent messages still need a tie-break). Use them only if you truly need the guarantee.
evidence: Ch10 §10.2: 'The overly complicated way: CRDTs ... and vector clocks ... It isn't worth it here ... you don't re-architect a system for one edge case.'

answer: Store important data with standby nodes and replication factor three: the write goes to one data node, which replicates it to two others, done by the DB's storage engine, not by workers (workers writing to several instances is worse). The DB never acknowledges a write until written in three places, so a write lost before that was never accepted (DynamoDB writes to three storage nodes; page note: it actually acks at 2 of 3). Re-reading Kafka isn't the way back (class: already processed; page note: Kafka retains events, but durability should come from the DB's replication).
evidence: Ch9 §9.5: 'important data is stored with standby nodes and a replication factor of three ... your DB would never say that I am done unless it is written in three different places'.
